title: Length-Weighted Loss Does Not Explain the Repetition Advantage in Long-CoT Supervised Fine-Tuning

contributions.purpose: Test the hypothesis that the Long-CoT 'repetition advantage' arises because per-sequence mean cross-entropy loss underweights long reasoning traces.
contributions.mechanism: Proposes a length-weighted loss L_len = (T/T_ref) * L_mean that upweights long sequences proportionally, tested against standard data scaling on OLMo3-7B.
contributions.evaluation: On AIME and GPQA, length-weighted loss achieves 25.5% accuracy, statistically identical to standard data scaling (25.6%) and recovering none of the 12.7-point gap (repetition: 38.3% at 1.6k samples x 32 epochs).
contributions.domain: Long chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning of LLMs
contributions.source_quote: We test whether length-weighted SFT loss explains the repetition advantage in Long-CoT fine-tuning, finding that it does not.

contributions.purpose: Establish that the negative result is robust across weighting schemes, not specific to one loss form.
contributions.mechanism: Systematic exploration of three distinct loss reweighting approaches: linear, quadratic, and token-level positional weighting.
contributions.evaluation: All three reweighting approaches fail to recover any meaningful fraction of the performance gap; stronger weighting also degrades performance.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that the negative result is robust: three distinct loss reweighting approaches (linear, quadratic, token-level) all fail to recover any meaningful fraction of the performance gap.

contributions.purpose: Redirect the explanation of the repetition advantage away from gradient signal distribution.
contributions.mechanism: Uses the negative results to eliminate gradient-signal-distribution explanations and argue for an alternative mechanism.
contributions.evaluation: Provides evidence the mechanism is not gradient signal distribution, pointing toward memorization convergence through repeated exposure (termination rate 90% vs 46%).
contributions.source_quote: We provide evidence that the repetition advantage mechanism is not gradient signal distribution, pointing toward memorization convergence through repeated exposure as the likely explanation.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Our work tests whether similar loss reweighting can explain the repetition advantage in Long-CoT SFT, finding that it cannot.

Kopiczko et al. (2026) demonstrate a surprising phenomenon in long chain-of-thought (Long-CoT) supervised fine-tuning: under a fixed optimizer-step budget, training for many epochs on a small dataset substantially outperforms single-epoch training on a proportionally larger dataset.

notes: Negative-result paper (stated in title and abstract): the hypothesis that length-weighted loss explains the repetition advantage is refuted; length-weighted loss (25.5%) is statistically identical to standard data scaling and recovers none of the 12.7-point gap, and quadratic/token-level weighting also fail or degrade performance.
